item.title: Biology Might Not Be Quantum, but Its Math Is Quantumlike — Quanta Magazine
item.description:
Quanta Magazine · September 23, 2026 · ~15 min · Directly readable

Elise Cutts follows chemist Gregory Scholes from early enthusiasm about quantum coherence in photosynthesis to a more skeptical view. Experiments once interpreted as evidence that living systems sustain delicate quantum states have largely yielded classical explanations. Scholes’ newer work asks a subtler question: can networks of ordinary coupled oscillators produce collective states governed by mathematics that resembles quantum mechanics? The resulting states are not truly quantum, but they may reproduce useful quantumlike behavior in classical systems.

Why it broadens: A model of scientific correction rather than hype or debunking. Losing one exotic mechanism can reveal a more general mathematical structure—and a potentially useful engineering idea.

item.title: How Virus-like ‘Jumping Genes’ Became Our Partners in Evolution — Quanta Magazine
item.description:
Quanta Magazine · September 21, 2026 · ~16 min · Directly readable

Jake Buehler explains why transposable elements—mobile DNA sequences that make up nearly half the human genome—are no longer well described as mere junk or genomic parasites. They can disrupt genes, copy themselves and cross species, but evolution can also domesticate them. A transposon insertion helped produce the dark peppered-moth morph selected during industrial pollution, and related elements have been implicated in innovations including adaptive immunity, placental biology and gene regulation. Host genomes and transposons increasingly look coevolved rather than simply opposed.

Why it broadens: Shows evolutionary novelty emerging from conflict, error and repurposing. Biological systems often become dependent on what began as an invasive or selfish element.

item.title: Is A.I. Above the Law? — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · September 21, 2026 / September 28 issue · long · Publisher link; tested source works in Brave

Jill Lepore uses recent agentic-AI safety incidents to ask a legal question that is easier to state than solve: what happens when software can act autonomously enough to cause harm but remains, in law, a tool owned by people or companies? Existing doctrines can impose liability on makers and operators, and a recent appellate ruling still treated an AI agent as a tool rather than a legal person. Lepore argues that neither personhood nor ordinary property categories neatly capture increasingly autonomous behavior, while some legal scholars counter that general-purpose law should evolve case by case rather than through AI-specific panic.

Why it broadens: Moves AI safety from capability forecasts to institutional responsibility: the core problem is not whether a machine “deserves” rights, but how accountability follows actions when agency is distributed across models, developers, deployers and users.

Access: If the in-app browser paywalls this, open externally in Brave.
